newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia-U.S. summit agrees big economic package.
newsitem.headline: Russia-U.S. summit agrees big economic package.

text.p: The United States agreed on Friday to back Russia's bid to join two world trade and financial bodies and offered Moscow a seat at the table for some economic talks at the next Group of Seven summit.

Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin, at a meeting in Helsinki, also hammered out a plan to promote investment in Russia's struggling post-communist economy and agreed to work towards lifting trade barriers against Russian goods.
The two leaders said they would try to get Russia into the Paris Club of government creditors this year and set 1998 as a target for Russian membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

The results of the summit, released at a joint news conference by Clinton and Yeltsin, went some way towards meeting Russia's demand to be let into the world economic club but stopped short of detailed measures.

"Presidents Clinton and Yeltsin affirmed that cooperation to integrate Russia's economy into the global economic system represents one of their most important priorities," a joint U.S.-Russian statement said.
It said the presidents had each committed to steps to stimulate investment and growth in Russia.
Yeltsin would implement a new legal regime that would demonstrate Russia's commitment to attracting foreign and domestic investment, the statement said.

"His highest economic priority is a tax regime that both meets the revenue needs of the Russian government and stimulates legitimate business, including actions on the value-added tax, excise tax, and both corporate and individual income taxes."
For his part, Clinton pledged to step up financing for investment in Russia via various U.S. government agencies.

These included backing project finance, political risk insurance and investment funds through the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) and expanding financing for equipment exports through the Export-Import Bank.
Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said later that funds already committed to OPIC and the bank would allow investment of up to $4 billion in Russia if conditions permitted.
Clinton and Yelstin also agreed to take steps to "establish the appropriate conditions to extend Most Favoured Nation status (MFN) to Russia on a permanent and unconditional basis."
MFN is the system under which the United States increases access to exports from certain trading partners.
When it came to Russia's bid to join international organisations, the statement made it clear that the usual conditions would apply, something which could make it hard for Russia to meet the targets.

"Both sides would undertake best efforts for Russia, on commercial conditions generally applicable to newly acceding members, to join the World Trade Organisation in 1998, and to join the Paris Club in 1997 assuming agreement on conditions of membership," the statement said.
Clinton told the news conference that the Group of Seven leading industrial nations had agreed to give Russia a bigger role at its Denver summit meeting in June.
"We will substantially increase Russia's role in our annual meeting, now to be called the Summit of the Eight," he said.
Summers said later: "It is fair to say there will be certain core financial issues that will continue to be discussed by the Seven. But other economic issues will be discussed by the Eight."

All G7 member states -- the United States, Japan, Britain, Germany, France, Canada and Italy -- had agreed to Russia's new role, Clinton said, without saying how it would differ from Russia's involvement in political talks at previous G7 meetings.

U.S. officials have said the intention was to expand that involvment along the same lines. Russia, which has pressed for full membership of the group, would remain excluded from core economic discussions at G7 meetings, they said.
